UK house prices rise at fastest pace in two years, says Halifax

Published 2026-10-07 07:05 UTC

UK house prices rose by 0.9% in September, the fastest monthly rise in two years, according to the Halifax, the UK's biggest mortgage lender. The average property now costs GBP 301,000, up 3.4% on a year earlier.

Amanda Bryden, head of mortgages at Halifax, said buyers had returned after mortgage rates fell over the summer, although affordability remained stretched for many first-time buyers. Prices rose in every region of the UK except London, where they were flat.

Economists cautioned that one strong month did not mark a turning point and said the outlook depended on whether the Bank of England continued cutting interest rates. Separate figures showed mortgage approvals rose for a third month in a row.

The lender said the average price of a UK home reached £301,000 last month, an annual rise of 4.8%. Prices rose in every region, with the strongest growth in Northern Ireland and the north-west of England, while London lagged behind with growth of under 2%.

Halifax said demand had been supported by falling mortgage rates, as lenders competed for business after a period of high borrowing costs. Average two-year fixed mortgage rates have fallen below 4.5% for the first time in more than two years, according to financial information firms.

First-time buyers have been particularly active, helped by rising wages and changes to lending rules that allow some borrowers to take larger loans relative to their incomes. However, many still struggle to save a deposit, and estate agents report that the supply of homes for sale remains tight in many areas.

Economists warned that the pace of growth may not last. Affordability remains stretched, with the average house price now around seven times average earnings. Some expect price growth to slow next year as the effect of lower mortgage rates fades and higher property taxes on second homes take effect.

Other measures of the housing market, including figures from Nationwide, have shown slightly slower growth, but all point to a recovery from the downturn of recent years.
